issues.issue: "Authorized University official" is undefined, so which employees may demand identification is left open. The provision also gives no consequence for an official who fails to reciprocate on request.
"Replaced as soon as possible" fixes no deadline and no benchmark against which delay could be measured. The distinction between a "damaged" card (free) and a "lost" card (fee) is likewise undefined.

The enumerated privileges (check cashing, elections, athletic events, library, campus technologies) are closed with "etc.", leaving the reach of the catch-all to ejusdem generis argument. "Properly entitled" is also undefined by any other provision.

"Influencing" another student to violate a standard has no boundary and is far broader than the neighboring verbs "enticing" and "enlisting". A court would have to decide whether mere influence, without solicitation, is sanctionable.

The sentence "communicating information important requests, updates, policies" is ungrammatical — a word or comma is missing — so what the e-mail account is the primary means of communicating is unclear. "Maintain currency with the use of" the account also states no measurable duty.

The section is hortatory — "all members share the responsibility" — and states no rule a student could be found to have violated. Whether it creates an enforceable standard at all, alongside the specific duties in 2.1–2.14, is open.

The prohibited behaviors — "intimidates", "harasses or bullies", "unwanted physical contact", "endangers the health, safety, or welfare" — are stated as bare verbs with no severity, intent, or reasonableness threshold. A student cannot tell from the words where ordinary conduct ends and a violation begins.

"Comply with instructions of University officials, committees, or boards" is unlimited in subject matter and contains no requirement that the instruction be lawful, reasonable, or within the official's authority. Its scope must be construed against the specific duties enumerated elsewhere in Section 2.

"Final decision" is ambiguous because 19.7 permits the University Appeals Board to conduct a new hearing and modify a Board decision, and 21.1 makes sanctions ineffective until approved. When a decision becomes "final" for purposes of this compliance duty is not stated.

"Legitimate functions" and "obstructing or disrupting" are undefined and could capture protected protest as easily as physical obstruction. The catch-all "or other authorized functions" extends an already open list.

"Causes disruption to" another individual's privacy is vague, and the provision does not say whose judgment of disruption controls. "Other electronic devices" is a catch-all appended to a list of specific devices.

"Issuing any type of threat is strictly prohibited" is a general prohibition of unlimited reach dropped into a provision otherwise confined to fire and safety equipment. Read ejusdem generis it means threats of a safety-equipment kind; read literally it prohibits any threat anywhere.

The protected categories listed here (race, sex, color, national origin, religion, age, gender, gender identity and expression, sexual orientation, disability, veteran status, genetic information) do not match the longer list in Section 7.0 and 7.3, which add ancestry, religious creed, ethnic origin and specific veteran statuses. Which list defines prohibited discrimination for a student charge is unresolved.

Hazing is defined only by example — "often in the nature of forced alcohol consumption, humiliating or painful ordeals" — so "initiating or disciplining fellow students" is the operative and unbounded term. "Often" signals that the examples do not limit the definition, leaving no boundary at all.

The catch-all "other articles or substances usable as weapons" follows a list of specific weapons and, read literally, covers kitchen knives, tools and chemicals. "Knives" itself is unqualified by blade length or purpose.

The guide-and-service-animal exception appears only in the second sentence, so on the face of the text the first sentence's leash requirement and the building-entry ban apply differently to service animals. Whether the exception carries back to the whole provision must be construed.

"Guest" is not defined anywhere in the code, so who counts as a student's guest — an invited visitor, anyone the student admits to a building — is open. The host's liability for "actions" of that person is correspondingly unbounded.

This provision incorporates by reference an open-ended class of "other official University publications and documents", identified only by examples introduced with "e.g.". Which outside documents become enforceable student-conduct standards is left to argument.

"Could be construed as retaliation" makes the test the possible construction of an observer rather than the actor's conduct or intent, and no severity threshold is given. The standard is markedly broader than the retaliation prohibition in 7.4, which requires action against a good-faith complainant.

"Sexual misconduct" is never defined in this section or elsewhere in the code, and the operative sentence says only that an interaction "could be defined as" misconduct if consent is absent. "Consent must be sought and clearly understood and communicated" does not say whether express words are required or whether conduct suffices.

The corresponding 3.0 in the 2013–2014 Rights and Responsibilities requires that consent "be sought affirmatively" and refers to "all parties" rather than "both parties"; a student whose conduct spans the editions faces two different consent standards. Nothing in this handbook says which edition governs conduct or an adjudication straddling academic years.

The provision sets two different consent standards in consecutive sentences — "explicit consent of each student involved" and consent "clearly communicated, mutual, non-coercive" — and says only that contact without it "may be considered" misconduct. "Explicit" is not defined, so whether silence or acquiescence can ever be consent is unresolved.

The 2013–2014 handbook's 3.1 requires consent "clearly and affirmatively communicated" and speaks of each "person" rather than each "student"; the two editions state materially different rules for the same conduct. Neither this provision nor any other says which edition applies to conduct or proceedings spanning both years.

This provision makes "taking advantage of someone's ... intoxication" misconduct, while 3.1 makes only a person "physically or mentally incapacitated" incapable of consent. Intoxication short of incapacity is thus prohibited here and permitted there, and the two cannot both be given effect.

Lack of consent may be inferred from advantage gained by the Accuser's "incapacity or impairment" of which the Accused "was aware or should have been aware" — "impairment" is a lower and undefined threshold than the "incapacity" defined in 3.1. The constructive-knowledge standard also gives no measure of what the Accused should have perceived.
"Students should report" is precatory and does not say whether reporting to Public Safety is a condition of any campus process. Whether this creates any obligation, or merely advice, is open.

This bullet says campus disciplinary proceedings "may be initiated" through the DSRCS, while 18.0 provides that disciplinary action "may be implemented only through the report of a violation" on a Community Standards Report. Whether an anonymous hotline call can initiate a proceeding, given 18.0's written-report requirement and the promise to show the CSR in its entirety to the Accused, is unresolved.

This bullet permits "passive assistance of legal counsel" only where "coexisting criminal charges are pending", whereas the Advisor definition in 22.6 allows an attorney to serve as Advisor whenever "co-existing criminal proceedings exist". A pending investigation without charges satisfies one formulation and not the other.

"Insofar as they relate to the Accuser" gives no criterion for which parts of an outcome are disclosable, and the promise sits against 19.10.N and P, which direct outcome notification only to the Accused. What the Accuser is entitled to learn must be construed from the two together.

"Any reasonably available changes in academic or living situations" states no standard for what is reasonably available and no obligation to make any change. The provision promises availability of staff, not accommodation.

"Highest standards of academic integrity" and "work that is falsified or is not the result of the student's own effort" set no ascertainable line, particularly for collaborative or edited work. The sanctions listed "or other sanctions" are also open-ended.

The provision breaks off mid-sentence at "Talking during an examination, or possession or use of", so the prohibition it was stating is textually incomplete. What is prohibited during an examination cannot be determined from these words.

"Appropriate posting materials that will not cause damage" is judged after the fact and by no stated standard. The provision names no approving authority for non-residential spaces beyond a cross-reference.

"Only sidewalks may be chalked" cannot be squared with the later sentence barring chalking "in areas where it cannot be washed away by the rain", which assumes covered areas might otherwise be chalkable. "Inappropriate" chalked messages is also an undefined ground for removal.

"Inappropriate use of property" is an undefined catch-all appended to specific wrongs like vandalism and theft. The extension to "personal and public property that surrounds the campus" has no geographic limit.

"Explicit permission" for storage closets, utility rooms and roof areas does not identify who may grant it or in what form. The general duty to observe "University guidelines and policies" incorporates unnamed documents.
"Mistreatment of animals, trees, or plantings" is undefined and gives no threshold — picking a flower and injuring an animal fall in the same words. No intent requirement is stated.

The protected-class list here (adding ancestry, religious creed, ethnic origin, Vietnam Era Veteran and "any other category protected by law") differs from the list in 2.7 and again from the list in 7.3. Which enumeration defines a chargeable discrimination offense cannot be settled from any one of them.

Harassment is "regarded as" occurring when conduct has "the purpose or effect of unreasonably interfering" with education or work, with no severity or pervasiveness requirement and no statement of whose perception governs. Because a single unwelcome remark can have that "effect", the boundary of the offense is left to case-by-case construction.

The list is expressly non-exhaustive ("includes, but is not limited to") and several entries — "leering", comments that "would otherwise tend to be degrading" — have no objective content. Whether conduct outside the enumerated examples can constitute sexual harassment, and by what test, is open.

The closing sentence — the University "may take action on conduct that it deems to be inappropriate, regardless of whether it rises to the level of a violation of law" — makes the University's own view of inappropriateness the operative standard. Combined with "This is not an exhaustive list", the provision states no boundary a student could rely on.

This retaliation rule protects only persons who complain of harassment or discrimination or cooperate in such an investigation, while 2.14 forbids anything "that could be construed as retaliation" for any good-faith report to Public Safety or the conduct process. The two prohibitions differ in trigger and breadth and are cross-referenced to each other as if identical.

"Falsified a claim" is not defined and is not distinguished from a claim merely found unsubstantiated. The provision also names no process or decision-maker for the determination, though dismissal is a possible consequence.

The heading limits this provision to concerns "Concerning Staff or Faculty", but the final sentence directs complaints against undergraduate and graduate students to the Dean of Student Life — a route that does not match 18.0, under which the Community Standards Report to the DSRCS is the official reporting mechanism for all student allegations. Which office a student complaint must be filed with is therefore doubtful.

"Malicious or unauthorized entry" into "personal files, electronic files" is undefined as to what authorization means for shared or networked spaces. The word "etc." extends the list of protected spaces without limit.

The advance-permission, particularity and receipt requirements here cannot easily be squared with 17.3, which permits periodic staff inspections of residence hall rooms on 24 hours' public notice with no statement of permission at all. Whether an "inspection" under 17.3 is a "search" governed by 17.2 is left to construction.

An inspection "to check for illegal possession of University-owned property" is investigative in purpose, yet it dispenses with the individualized permission, particularity and receipt safeguards required by 17.2 for searching a student's room. The two provisions describe overlapping intrusions under different rules.

This provision hands the content of a student's records rights to an external document, the Brandeis University Records Policy, which is not reproduced or incorporated by its terms. Its access rules must then be reconciled with the seven-year retention and confidentiality rules in 19.5 and 19.6.j.

"In a timely manner" and "not reported in a timely fashion" fix no limitations period, yet untimeliness is a ground for refusing to refer a case. There is no benchmark against which the delay of a report could be measured.

The statement that disciplinary action "may be implemented only through the report of a violation to the [DSRCS]" cannot be squared with 22.1, 22.3 and 22.4, under which the Dean may remove, suspend, or dismiss a student with no report at all. Which route is exclusive is unresolved.

The subject matter suited to mediation is a non-exhaustive list ("includes, though is not limited to") that does not exclude allegations under Section 3 or 7, although 3.0, 7.0 and 22.6 require that such allegations be adjudicated by the Special Examiner's Process. Whether a sexual misconduct allegation may be mediated instead cannot be answered from either provision alone.

"Impasse or other impediment" is judged solely by the Director with no standard stated, and "further mediation or referral to the conduct process" leaves the consequence of non-compliance unfixed. This sits against 18.1's statement that a mediated outcome is "final, and binding".

The provision directs that where a student fails to choose, the administrator "may proceed to sanctioning in accordance with Section 19.3", but 19.3 governs failure to attend a meeting after choosing Administrative Action and prescribes no sanctioning procedure. The cross-reference identifies no rule that can be applied.

"Under the Administrative Action option, this is the only opportunity to present evidence" cannot be squared with 19.8, which entitles the Accused to meet the Dean to "discuss an administrative decision" and permits amendment of the decision. Whether information offered at the Dean's review counts as evidence is left open.

The administrator "may complete the process in the student's absence" while the same provision guarantees "the right to one rescheduled meeting" for a blameless absence, with no sequencing between the two. Whether a decision rendered before that right is exercised is valid must be construed.

The power to defer proceedings on account of a student's withdrawal cannot be squared with 22.6, which provides that once the Special Examiner's Process is activated by a CSR "it may not be interrupted by the withdrawal from the University by the Accused". Nothing states that 19.4 is inapplicable to Section 3 and 7 cases.

Records are destroyed after seven years "except in extraordinary cases as defined by the Dean of Student Life", a standard the Dean defines after the fact and which appears nowhere else in the code. The retention period is therefore indefinite at the Dean's option.

"Within 30 class days, or as soon as practicable" makes the deadline elastic, since the alternative swallows the rule and has no measure. The definition of "class days" here (excluding summer and study abroad) also differs from 19.2, where final exams and Senior Week count as class days.

The Hearing Administrator is to ensure execution of the hearing "as prescribed in Section 23", but this code contains no Section 23; the hearing procedures are in 19.10. The governing procedural reference is therefore missing.

The bar on parties "confronting or questioning the witnesses and Accusers regarding the case prior to the hearing" cannot be squared with 19.6.e, which makes it "the responsibility of the Accuser and the Accused to notify their witnesses ... regarding the time, date, and location of the hearing". A party must contact witnesses it is forbidden to approach.

This provision lets "the Accused and Accuser" agree to proceed without the prescribed minimum voting composition, while 20.2 requires that the voting requirements be waived "by mutual consent of the SCB, the Accuser, and the Accused". Whether the Board's consent is also needed cannot be answered from either provision alone.

"Passive assistance" is never defined, and the same provision allows the Hearing Administrator to permit "active participation by an Advisor" in "exceptional circumstances" that are not described. What an Advisor may actually do at a hearing is thus indeterminate.

The requirement that both parties be present is qualified "except as provided in Section 19.16.k", a section that does not exist in this code (the rescheduling rule is 19.6.k). The exception to the attendance requirement therefore points nowhere.

"Unduly repetitious or irrelevant" evidence may be excluded by the Board on no stated standard, and the provision expressly disclaims the rules of evidence that would supply one. What governs admissibility is left entirely to the Board.

The right "to question all witnesses appearing before the Board and only at the hearing" guaranteed here has no counterpart in the Special Examiner's Process of 22.6, which routes all Section 3 and 7 cases to an investigator who interviews witnesses separately and privately. Whether a student charged under Sections 3 or 7 retains any questioning right is unresolved by the two provisions read together.

The phrase "and only at the hearing" is grammatically attached to the right to question witnesses, so it can be read either as limiting when questioning may occur or as limiting which witnesses may be questioned. The following sentences, which admit written testimony from absentee witnesses, make the choice consequential.

Placing the burden of proof on the Accuser cannot be squared with 22.6, where the Special Examiner investigates and reports and the Dean applies a preponderance standard with no burden assigned to any party. For Section 3 and 7 cases the two allocations of proof cannot both operate.

A finding of responsibility here may be made "based only upon clear and convincing evidence", while the Standard of Evaluation in 22.6 directs that the Special Examiner's Process use preponderance of the evidence. Identical conduct is thus judged by two different standards depending on which section is charged, with no rule for mixed charges.

A blameworthy failure to attend means the Accused "shall be deemed to have accepted the responsibility", converting an absence into an admission with no finding on the merits. The provision gives the same right to a rescheduled hearing to the Accuser but imposes the deeming consequence only on the Accused.

This provision requires that sanctions "shall not take effect until approved or modified by the Dean ... or the Director", whereas the Special Examiner's Process provides that all sanctions "will be in effect immediately, regardless of any appeal". A student appealing under one regime is stayed and under the other is not, and nothing reconciles them.

The 2-business-day window runs from "delivery of the conduct action announcement" without saying what constitutes delivery, whereas 19.1 and 19.7 specify delivery in person, to the Brandeis e-mail account, or to the home address. When the clock starts is therefore uncertain.

Requiring students who learn of possible new evidence at the hearing to seek a continuance "rather than wait to raise the matter ... as the basis for an appeal request" operates as a waiver of the new-evidence ground expressly given by 19.7.d. Whether failing to ask for a continuance forfeits that appeal ground is not stated.

The philosophy and procedures the Chairperson explains are contained in a separate statement "available from the Department of Student Rights and Community Standards" that is not reproduced in the code. What is read to the parties is therefore governed by an external document of unknown content.

The enumerated "Rights to Fairness" — an Advisor, presenting witnesses, questioning witnesses appearing against them, verbal argument, silence — are stated as the parties' rights "under this process", yet none of them is provided in the Special Examiner's Process of 22.6, to which all Section 3 and 7 cases are sent. Whether these are University-wide fairness guarantees or only Board-hearing steps is precisely what the two provisions leave open.

The accusations read to the hearing come from the Choice of Action Form, whereas 19.1 provides that the student receives "written charges" after the Preliminary Meeting. Which document fixes the charges to be tried is not stated.

The Accused accepts or denies responsibility again at the hearing although 19.1 provides that a choice has already been made and that failure to choose "constitutes an acceptance of responsibility". What happens if the two answers differ is not addressed.

The Accused's right to question the Accuser directly at the hearing has no analogue in the Special Examiner's Process, under which Section 3 and 7 cases proceed with separate private interviews. Whether the right survives the routing rule in 3.0 and 22.6 is unresolved.

"Witnesses for the Accuser may be called" does not say who decides whether they are called, while 19.6.e conditions testimony on availability and 19.6.b leaves unlisted witnesses to the Chairperson's discretion. Whether a party may compel the calling of its own listed witness is left open.

Recall and re-questioning follow "the same order as previous witness questioning", but the orders in steps G and H are opposites, so which order governs a recalled witness is indeterminate. The provision also does not say who decides that a recall is permitted.

A finding of not responsible is announced to the parties yet the outcome notification is "pending approval by the Dean of Student Life or an Associate Dean", implying an acquittal may be withheld — while 21.1 makes Deans' approval a condition only of sanctions. Whether a not-responsible finding is final when announced cannot be settled from either provision alone.

Final sanction determinations are communicated in writing "to the Accused" only, although the Section 3 services bullet promises that the Accuser will be informed of the outcome of proceedings insofar as it relates to the Accuser. The two provisions state different disclosure obligations for the same event.

The Board is advised of the Accused's past conduct history during deliberations, although 19.6.i requires that "decisions shall be based solely upon evidence and testimony introduced at the hearing". Whether that limitation applies to the sanctioning deliberation as well as the responsibility finding is unresolved.

"The appropriate administrator" who reviews the Board's recommendations is not identified, while 21.1 names three officials who may approve or modify sanctions and 19.10.P names a further set. Who holds the reviewing authority must be pieced together from other provisions.

The SCB's jurisdiction excludes "cases related to Sections 3 and 7", but the code gives no rule for a case that charges both a Section 3 or 7 violation and violations of other sections such as 2.1. Whether the whole case goes to the Special Examiner or is split between two processes is left open.

The waiver here requires "mutual consent of the SCB, the Accuser, and the Accused", while 19.6.c allows the Accused and Accuser alone to agree to proceed without the prescribed minimum voting composition. The two provisions state different requirements for the same waiver.

The sentence "Staff members appointed by the Senior Vice President for Students and Enrollment" omits its verb, so whether staff appointment is mandatory or merely descriptive is uncertain. The provision also gives no size for the pool it requires.

"A representative cross-section of Brandeis students" states no criterion of representativeness and no consequence if the Board is not so composed. The selection "process open to all continuing students" is likewise undescribed.

"Chaired by students, each annually selected by the Board and the DSRCS Director" does not say how many Chairpersons there are or who chairs a given hearing. 19.6.i and 20.6 both assume a single Chairperson with distinct powers.

Removal turns on "behavior that conflicts with the high standards of citizenship, confidentiality, and cooperation that the Board represents" — a standard with no defined content and no process. Nothing states who determines the behavior occurred.

This provision states that "An Associate Dean of Student Life will serve as Chairperson of the University Appeals Board", while 20.8 provides that the Chairperson shall be a full-time tenured faculty member appointed by the Dean. The two cannot both be given effect as to who chairs the UAB.

The requirement of "one faculty Chairperson" who is a full-time tenured faculty member contradicts 20.7, under which an Associate Dean of Student Life serves as Chairperson of the UAB. Nothing in either provision resolves which appointment controls.

"Selected in a manner similar to that of the SCB" incorporates the SCB rules of 20.3–20.5 only by analogy, though 20.8 prescribes different appointing authorities and eligibility for the UAB. What "similar" requires is left to construction.

Removal turns on "behavior that conflicts with the high standards of citizenship, confidentiality, and cooperation that the UAB represents", a standard with no stated content. The Chairperson consulted is also identified differently by 20.7 and 20.8.

The sanctioning factors are "including but not limited to" and the learning-component list is likewise open, so a sanction may rest on considerations found nowhere in the code. Items such as "Failure in a course or on an assignment" and "Family notification" are punitive rather than learning components, blurring the category the list is said to illustrate.

The rule that sanctions "shall not take effect until approved" by a named official cannot be squared with the Special Examiner's Process, under which all sanctions, including suspension and dismissal, "will be in effect immediately, regardless of any appeal". Whether Section 21's approval condition applies to Section 3 and 7 outcomes is unresolved.

"No Further Action" still records a responsible finding in the student's DSRCS record, so whether it is a sanction at all — and therefore appealable under 19.7 — is unclear. "Sufficient in-and-of itself" states no criterion.

"Additional conditions may be applied as appropriate" converts a written warning into an open-ended sanction with no stated limit. What conditions may accompany the least severe sanction is left wholly to the administrator.

"Would normally be taken after one serious violation or repeated violations related to the living unit environment" is descriptive rather than a condition, so removal is not actually limited to those cases. "Serious violation" is undefined.

The privileges that may be denied are "including, but not limited to" a list of specific campus benefits, leaving the catch-all's reach — for instance to academic or housing benefits — to ejusdem generis argument. "A specific period of time" is required but no maximum is set.

Probation may be revoked if the student "in any way fail[s] to conduct themselves as a responsible member of the University community" — a condition with no ascertainable content beyond the conduct rules themselves. The probationary term is only "usually" stated.

The sentence "Suspension may extend for a semester, until a designated date, and/or until degrees/certificates will not be issued and credit will not be granted for courses taken elsewhere" is textually broken; words are plainly missing after "until". As written the definition of the duration and effect of Suspension cannot be applied.

The power to "take any action that it believes to be appropriate and reasonable" whenever the University "has reason to believe" conduct "may disrupt" safety or well-being cannot be squared with 22.2, which forbids altering a student's status or suspending campus access except for "imminent danger". One provision requires imminent danger and the other requires only a belief in possible disruption.

"After any removal" is not limited to removals under 22.1, so on its face it also governs returns after emergency suspension under 22.2, indefinite suspension under 22.3 and suspension imposed as a sanction under 21.1.g — which requires a further approval by the Committee on Academic Standing. The scope of the Dean's exclusive authority is therefore uncertain.

The student has 3 business days to seek a meeting but no deadline is fixed for the Dean to meet or to decide, so an interim removal may continue indefinitely. Whether the action remains in force during the contest is not stated.

Emergency suspension is permitted here only for "imminent danger", while 3.0 and 2.1.f state that any student merely accused of sexual misconduct or involved in a personal-rights incident "may be placed on campus restriction or emergency suspension pending the outcome of any investigation". The two conditions for the same measure conflict.

"Charged with or convicted of a crime" is unlimited as to the nature of the offense, so a minor infraction triggers the same power as a felony, subject only to the Dean's duty to "consider" the nature of the crime. The provision also expressly disapplies the procedural standards of Section 19 while allowing indefinite suspension.

Discipline up to dismissal turns on off-campus behavior that "in the judgment of the Dean" is inconsistent with being a "good citizen and good neighbor" and "adversely affects the University community" — standards with no ascertainable content. The provision expressly removes the Section 19 procedures that would otherwise supply a check.

"Severe emotional or psychological distress" and conduct "result[ing] in the intervention" of a health provider are undefined triggers for a mandatory emergency protocol. Whether voluntarily seeking counseling can trigger the protocol is not addressed.

The student is given 3 business days to seek a meeting but the Dean is given no deadline to decide, and the protocol's restrictions continue meanwhile. Whether the right to contest has any practical operation is left unstated.

The absolute exclusion from campus with "no exception for examinations or other time-sensitive ... academic obligations" cannot be squared with the preceding paragraph's promise of a meeting to contest the protocol and possible restoration of privileges. The bar operates fully before any contest can be heard.

The routing rule sends a case to the Special Examiner's Process whenever "one or more possible violations" of Sections 3 or 7 exist, but 20.1 gives the Student Conduct Board jurisdiction over violations of all other standards. Which process adjudicates the non-Section-3/7 charges in a mixed case is unresolved.

The promise that "the CSR will be shown, in its entirety, to the accused student(s)" sits against the Statements Phase rule that the Accused "will not be shown the Accuser's detailed statement" until after responding. What the Accused is entitled to see, and when, cannot be settled from either provision alone.

An attorney may hold the Advisor role "when co-existing criminal proceedings exist", while 19.6.d and the Section 3 services bullet permit counsel only where "coexisting criminal charges are pending". Whether an uncharged police investigation qualifies turns on which formulation governs.

Routing is decided by the Director "in conjunction with the Dean of Student Life", although the opening paragraph of 22.6 assigns the determination to the DSRCS and 18.0 assigns the referral judgment to "the administrator in the DSRCS". Who actually decides which process a report enters is stated three different ways.

The Special Examiner is defined as investigator and author of "findings", while the Special Examiner's Report paragraph says the report merely "may offer conclusions or recommendations" and the Dean's definition says the Dean renders the Final Decision "after receiving the findings". Whether the Examiner or the Dean finds the facts and determines responsibility cannot be settled from these provisions read together.

"Currently or formerly a member of the Student Conduct Board or formerly of the University Appeals Board" is a garbled qualification whose two limbs use different tenses for no stated reason. It is also unclear whether a sitting SCB member may serve as Observer given 19.6.d's disqualification of Board members from party-side roles.

"Direct knowledge of the incident" is narrower than 19.6.e's witness definition ("information directly related to the incident"), so a person who may testify before the Board is not necessarily a witness in the Special Examiner's Process. Which definition governs a Section 3 or 7 case is not stated.

The Dean renders the Final Decision here and also receives the UAB's report and "retain[s] the discretion to amend or uphold" that decision on appeal, whereas 20.7 provides that the UAB "shall hear appeals of ... the Special Examiner's Process". The same official is thus both the decision-maker and the appellate authority.

The UAB here only "receive[s] any appeal ... and make[s] a report of its opinions to the Dean", while 20.7 says the UAB "shall hear appeals" of Special Examiner's Process decisions and 19.7 empowers it to uphold, reverse or change a sanction. Whether the UAB decides or merely advises cannot be answered from either provision alone.

The preponderance standard prescribed here conflicts with 19.6.i, under which a finding of responsibility may be made "based only upon clear and convincing evidence". Nothing states which standard governs a case charging both Section 3 or 7 and other violations.

The 60-day period is only "the goal of the University" and is qualified by "as soon as is practicable if unusual circumstances exist", so no enforceable time limit is created. "Unusual circumstances" is undefined and self-assessed.

The Accuser's full statement is requested only "if the contents of the initial report do not represent a full account", a judgment left entirely to the Special Examiner, so the charging document may be the CSR alone. Calling this "the principal opportunity" for the Accuser also leaves unstated what further opportunities exist.

The Accuser is promised "ample dialog" about an enumerated list of supports (counseling, academic support, living arrangements, travel), while the parallel paragraph for the Accused promises only unspecified "ongoing efforts to support the student". What the University owes each party differs on the face of the two paragraphs.

The rule that "the Accused will not be shown the Accuser's detailed statement until the Accused has written their own detailed response" cannot be squared with the promise that the CSR is shown "in its entirety" and with 19.1's requirement that the student be informed of "the details of the charges". What notice the Accused is entitled to before responding is left in doubt.

The statement that the process "may not be interrupted by the withdrawal from the University by the Accused" cannot be squared with 18.0, which limits disciplinary action to persons enrolled "up to and including the student's commencement day", or with 19.4's deferral for withdrawn students. Whether a withdrawn student remains subject to adjudication is unresolved.

An acceptance of responsibility here leads directly to a Dean-issued outcome with no statement of whether the resulting sanction may be appealed under the Appeals Procedures, which allow appeal only of "the Final Decision". Whether an accepted-responsibility outcome is a Final Decision is not addressed.

"Fails to cooperate" is undefined yet its consequence is that the Special Examiner "may consider the Accused to have accepted responsibility" — an admission by default with no finding on the merits. The provision does not say what conduct falls short of cooperation.

Evidence is to be "shared equally with the parties to ensure the opportunity for response", yet the same paragraph reserves the Examiner's discretion "not to share certain records due to confidentiality concerns". Only evidence the Examiner deems "of material importance" is shared at all, so the promise of response is qualified twice over.

The Special Examiner alone "will determine who will be interviewed, as well as how many times, and in what order", which cannot be squared with the right of the parties to present witnesses recognized in 19.10.C and 19.6.e for other conduct cases. Whether a party in a Section 3 or 7 case can compel any witness to be heard is unanswered.

The Observer's role is described only as "passive" with no statement of what the Observer may record or report, and no consequence if no Observer attends. The Advisor's entitlement to attend is stated without the "passive assistance" limits found in 19.6.d.

A "good-faith effort to contact all pertinent witnesses" sets no benchmark for effort and leaves pertinence to the Examiner's own judgment. Interviews may also be conducted by telephone or Internet tools with no rule for evaluating such testimony.

The report "may offer conclusions or recommendations as to the credibility of testimony or potential outcomes", making the central finding optional, while the Special Examiner definition says the Examiner prepares "findings" and the Dean definition says the Dean decides "after receiving the findings". Who resolves credibility and responsibility is left indeterminate.

The Discussion Phase gives the parties a meeting to "hear and respond to the findings" without saying whether the Special Examiner's report itself is provided to them. What a party is responding to is therefore undefined.

The Dean's decision whether to seek further fact-finding on newly submitted information is wholly discretionary, and the provision does not say whether a supplemental report is shared with the parties before decision. The 2-business-day window for new information is fixed while the Dean's response is not.

The Final Decision is due "no earlier than 4 business days, and usually within 7 business days", so the outer limit is only a usual practice rather than a deadline. "Binding" also sits oddly against the Appeals Procedures that follow.

Withdrawal of the allegation "will terminate the Special Examiner's Process", yet the University "reserves the right to take actions against the Accused outside of the Special Examiner's Process" — although 3.0, 7.0 and 22.6 require that Section 3 and 7 allegations be adjudicated by that process. What action may be taken, and under what procedure, is unstated.

An acceptance of responsibility is "non-reversible" and prompts an outcome, but the Appeals Procedures allow appeal on grounds including fraud and denial of rights without excepting such cases. Whether a student who accepted responsibility may still appeal is left open.

The Dean makes the responsibility finding by "application of the preponderance of the evidence standard" although the Dean neither interviews the parties nor takes testimony, and the Special Examiner's report need only "offer conclusions or recommendations". How the Dean applies the standard to a record compiled by another is not addressed by either provision.

Making all sanctions, "including suspension or dismissal", effective immediately "regardless of any appeal" cannot be squared with 19.7 and 21.1, under which sanctions do not take effect until approved or modified. It also leaves the appeal rights that follow with no practical remedy if granted.

The ground "denial of rights under this process" has no referent, because Section 22.6 nowhere enumerates the parties' rights in the way that 19.10.C sets out the "Rights to Fairness" for Board hearings. What rights an appellant may claim were denied must be constructed from elsewhere in the code.

The Special Examiner "will respond in writing to the appeal" even where the appeal alleges procedural error or denial of rights by that Examiner, and the provision gives the appellee only 4 business days while fixing no time for the Examiner's response. The appellee's response is also due "before the UAB makes any statements" rather than by a certain date.

The UAB's function here is to submit "opinions, thoughts, and suggestions" to the Dean, which cannot be squared with 20.7's provision that the UAB "shall hear appeals" of Special Examiner's Process decisions or with 19.7's power to reverse or change sanctions. The appellate body's authority differs between the two sections.

The Dean whose Final Decision is under appeal "retain[s] the discretion to amend or uphold" it after reading the UAB report, whereas 20.7 and 19.7 vest appellate determination in the University Appeals Board. Which body decides the appeal cannot be answered from either provision alone.

Records of the Special Examiner's Process are retained "pursuant to the rules in Sections 17.4, 19.5, and 19.6.j", which are drafted for Administrative Action records and Board Hearing Reports rather than for investigative reports. Which of those inconsistent regimes applies to an Examiner's report and interview notes is unstated.
